newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arafat hopes Egypt-Israel summit revives peace.
newsitem.headline: Arafat hopes Egypt-Israel summit revives peace.

text.p: Egypt and Israel prepared for a summit on Tuesday that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said he hoped would lead to a resumption of Middle East peacemaking.

Egypt made clear it would champion the Palestinian side when President Hosni Mubarak and Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meet in Sharm el-Sheikh, but would listen to any ideas on reviving Middle East peace.

Arafat, who held talks late on Monday in Cairo with Mubarak to coordinate views before the summit, told Israel's daily Haaretz he hoped it would revive Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations deadlocked for more than two months.
"The problem isn't building for Palestinians, rather halting the settlements," Arafat said.

Netanyahu has refused any halt. But after plunging peace moves into crisis in March when it broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, Israel last week approved building homes for Arabs opposite the site.
Arafat forecast a "disaster" unless Israel and his PLO made progress in peacemaking. Asked if he feared a war, he said: "Not only war, but confusion in all of the Middle East."

The contradictory views on Jewish settlements on Arab land occupied since 1967 have halted Palestinian-Israeli peace talks. The U.S. ambassador to Israel said he did not expect breakthroughs in Egypt.

"The issue is settlements. (Tuesday's) meeting is very important because we're talking about how to remedy the flaws in the peace process on specific bases...the Oslo and Madrid peace accords," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told reporters ahead of the summit at the Red Sea resort.

He was referring to the 1991 Middle East peace conference in Madrid at which Israel and the Palestinians agreed to trade occupied lands for peace -- a formula Netanyahu now rejects -- and the 1993 Oslo accord that mapped out the route to a final Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement.
"Arafat has articulated his point of view to us well. We're going to talk to him (Netanyahu) and we're going to listen to what he has to say or wishes to say," Moussa added.

"The Palestinians say they cannot negotiate against a background of fait accomplis and the continuation of settlements. Our job is to deal with that in order to pave the way for the resumption of a positive atmosphere which will enable us to save the peace process."
Arafat refuses to talk peace with Israel until it stops building a new Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem, captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
But Netanyahu says he will not stop building Jewish settlements and the Palestinians must end extremist violence before he will negotiate.

The Israeli prime minister said the issue of settlements was not on his agenda for Tuesday's meeting with Mubarak but Moussa told reporters Netanyahu had some views "he has not divulged before" to discuss with Mubarak.
"There's a lot that can happen at the meeting and we hope it will lead to the resumption of the peace process," he added.

Asked if he thought either Arafat or Netanyahu would compromise, Moussa said: "We hope so, meaning Netanyahu. The question is saving the peace and peace is incompatible with changes, fait accomplis and settlements."
